title: When Are Multimodal Predictions Biologically Supported? A Diagnostic Evaluation Framework
claim: A model-agnostic diagnostic stage maps any multimodal model's embeddings through four tests to one of several interpretable scenario verdicts.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; 2x2 metric grid feeding colored outcome boxes
description: A three-column diagram read left to right. The left column, "Paired data", shows a pathology whole-slide image and a gene-expression heatmap. Each feeds a trapezoid encoder box labeled Image or Expr., and both are marked with a snowflake for frozen. The middle column, "Multimodal model", contrasts Entangled models (CLIP, CCA), drawn as image and expression points aligned in one oval space, with Factorized models (JIVE, DSSL), drawn as X = shared + specific equations. Pink and blue paired squares represent per-modality embeddings, which feed the right column, "DECAT evaluation". That column has a 2x2 grid of dashed boxes: I. Structure, II. Signal, III. Locality and IV. Stability. Each box has a small plot, a formula and a short caption. Arrows lead from the grid to five rounded, colored outcome boxes: S1 Shared, S2 Spurious, S3 No signal, S4 Modality-specific and Indeterminate.
caption: DECAT framework overview. DECAT takes per-modality embeddings from any multimodal model and uses a four-stage decision tree to classify the predictive behavior of each modality, for a given task, into one of four scenarios or indeterminate (Figure [ref], Appendix [ref]). Scenario classification informs downstream decisions: cross-modally supported signal consistent with shared biology (S1) supports cross-modal deployment, modality-specific signal (S4) restricts reliable predictions to the source modality, spurious signal (S2) transfers across cohorts but exhibits composition-dependent instability indicating risk of failure under distribution shift, and no signal (S3) indicates the representation is uninformative for that task.
abstract: Multimodal models in oncology can produce accurate predictions, but accurate prediction does not reveal whether the model has learned biology that is shared across modalities, biology confined to one modality, or spurious correlations that reflect confounders rather than genuine biology. We introduce DECAT, a model-agnostic post-hoc evaluation framework that classifies multimodal representations into four diagnostic scenarios (shared, spurious, modality-specific, or no signal) for a given task and modality, using five null-referenced metrics and a rule-based decision procedure. The framework operates on learned representations, requires no knowledge of which specific confounder is present, and returns indeterminate when the evidence is insufficient. We evaluate multimodal architecture properties using DECAT on synthetic data across four multimodal model classes spanning over 2,500 trained representations, and demonstrate its operational use on 8,979 TCGA patients with both multimodal model embeddings and five pretrained pathology foundation models. Entangled models (e.g., CLIP) detect shared signal near-perfectly on synthetic data but also falsely claim it when it is absent, doing so in the majority of such cases on real foundation model embeddings. This false claim rate increases with signal strength and sample size, so that larger cohorts and stronger representations produce more confident but still incorrect diagnoses. Applied to both multimodal TCGA embeddings and five pathology foundation models without paired RNA, DECAT detects confounding invisible to AUROC without requiring the confounder labels, as confirmed by post-hoc stratification.
